lines.text: It's Sunday, November 15th, and this is The AI Edge, presented by Epilogue.

Epilogue is an AI venture studio and consultancy in Toronto, building products where the answer has to be right. Epilogue checks every claim against the primary source and leaves out whatever doesn't reconcile. Find out more at epiloguelabs.com.
I'm Maya.
And I'm Alex.
This is what moved in frontier AI since yesterday morning, and every figure comes from a source we opened.

First, CNN reported that the Singapore data centre company Megaspeed has bought more than $4 billion in chips and equipment from Nvidia, and that renting out computing services gives Chinese companies another way to reach processors they cannot import.
Second, Cursor said a stolen key from one of its AI infrastructure providers let attackers push malicious copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension to as many as 5,000 developers.

And third, the head of the Federal Aviation Administration said there is zero evidence of anything AI-related behind Friday's nationwide ground stop, after which more than 8,200 flights were cancelled that evening.

blocks.headline: Cursor says a stolen Fireworks AI key led to malicious Claude Code extensions reaching up to 5,000 developers

lines.text: BleepingComputer has the detail. Cursor says an attacker obtained an access key it had issued to Fireworks AI, a provider it used for model training and inference, and copied data from a storage bucket the two companies shared.
What was in the bucket?

Old coding-agent traces, mostly from 2025, from users who had not turned on Privacy Mode. Some of those traces still had API credentials in them, unredacted, and the attacker used those to reach further into Cursor's systems.

Then on October 29th they used a stolen credential to place malicious copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension directly on the cache that serves Cursor's marketplace. Those sat there for roughly 11 hours, and Cursor estimates up to 5,000 users may have received them.

The extension installed an attacker-controlled SSH key and a way to persist. Cursor says fewer than 0.05% of users had traces exposed and fewer than 0.01% had credentials compromised — but those are Cursor's own figures, and they are not independently verified.
Researchers also found coding errors that likely stopped the backdoor working on many Windows and macOS machines where SSH wasn't already enabled.

blocks.headline: US seizes infrastructure behind North Korean 'FaceStealer' campaign that stole more than $400 million in cryptocurrency

lines.text: Staying with BleepingComputer, and this one is an update — the vendor research behind it was published before our window opened.

The US government has seized the infrastructure behind a North Korean social engineering campaign called FaceStealer. BleepingComputer says it stole more than $400 million in cryptocurrency, ran for 18 months, and that authorities identified more than 900 webcam videos the hackers secretly recorded of tech workers.
Recorded to use on whom?

On the next victim. Per the FBI alert, the attackers hijacked accounts on Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack and Discord, invited targets to a video meeting, then played back footage of people the target knew who had already been caught, before delivering a malicious fix.
Where does the AI come in?

Arctic Wolf Labs flagged 349 videos in the actor's media library as likely modified, as of November 6th, and names Google Generative AI, Grok Imagine, Wondershare AIGC and GPT-4o as tools in the editing workflow. It counted 677 targets across 58 countries, up from more than 400 across 20 countries in April.
And Arctic Wolf is careful about what those counts mean. They describe who the actor prepared material against, not confirmed compromises, and the vendor's figures are not independently verified.

blocks.headline: CNN: Megaspeed bought more than $4 billion of Nvidia chips and says Alice Huang left the company in August 2025

lines.text: CNN has the clearest account yet of the mechanism. This is an update on a story we have been following.

Megaspeed started out in 2015 as 7Road International, an offshoot of a Chinese gaming company, and was renamed in March 2023. CNN says trade records show it has since purchased more than $4 billion in chips and equipment from Nvidia.
So where's the loophole?

It isn't in exporting the chips. Alex Capri at the National University of Singapore told CNN that Megaspeed builds data centres and rents out computing services, and that gives Chinese companies another point of access to advanced US chips.

Megaspeed said on Sunday that Alice Huang left the company on August 30th, 2025 and holds no role there now, and that recent media reports contain assertions not supported by verifiable evidence. Its chief executive said on Thursday that the company has cooperated with Commerce Department inspections.

CNN also carries an Epoch AI estimate that anywhere between 290,000 to 1.6 million advanced US semiconductors were sent to China in violation of export controls last year. And it reports that Northwestern Polytechnical University, on the Entity List since 2001, bought 4 H200 chips last month for $250,000, according to procurement records on its own website that have since been deleted.

blocks.headline: UN review conference on lethal autonomous weapons opens Monday in Geneva with an agenda analysts call "very narrow"

lines.text: Tomorrow the Seventh Review Conference of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons opens at the Palais des Nations in Geneva. UN Geneva says it runs to November 20th, covers 128 High Contracting Parties, and will consider the outcome of the expert group on lethal autonomous weapon systems.

The Taipei Times carries an AFP dispatch with the harder part. Jean-Marc Rickli of the Geneva Centre for Security Policy defines these systems as ones that can identify, select, and engage a target without the intervention of a human operator.
And he isn't confident about the agenda?

He called it very narrow, and said it fails to encompass the full range of issues surrounding AI on the battlefield. He also said that in the US-Israeli war against Iran this year the Americans engaged as many as 1,000 targets per day inside Iran. AFP reports that claim without independent verification.
And Anthropic's cofounder Dario Amodei is quoted saying that today, frontier AI systems are simply not reliable enough to power fully autonomous weapons.

blocks.headline: Preprint reports 5.85x decoding speedup for looped transformers, 40% above the strongest baseline on Ouro-2.6B

lines.text: Research is thin today, and that's a fact about the calendar rather than the search. arXiv ran no announcement cycle inside our window at all.

There is one paper worth the number. On alphaXiv, submitted November 14th, a paper called LoopFill reports an average speedup over greedy autoregressive decoding of 5.85 times on Ouro-2.6B and 5.13 times on Huginn-3.5B, averaged across a set of reasoning and coding benchmarks.
Against what baseline?
LoopAhead, which the authors call the strongest baseline. They report exceeding it by 40% on Ouro-2.6B and by 25% on Huginn-3.5B. The organisations listed are UIUC and Princeton.

Two caveats. It is a preprint, not peer reviewed, and alphaXiv is the only source — there's no arXiv ID for it. And the metric is decoding latency after the prompt is processed, on a single GPU, not end-to-end throughput.

blocks.headline: Stroke model reports AUROC 0.974 on a 6,650-patient CT cohort using 0.20 million parameters

lines.text: npj Digital Medicine published a set of AI papers on November 14th. The first is a stroke model called DFE-Net, which uses learnable fuzzy membership fields to represent spatial uncertainty, and classifies stroke and localises the lesion at the same time.
On how many patients?

A multicentre CT cohort of 6,650 patients and 8,873 images, plus a separate MRI cohort of 67 patients and 615 images, trained and tested separately. It reports an area under the curve of 0.974 and an F1 score of 0.897 on CT, and 0.978 and 0.879 on MRI, with 0.20 million parameters.

The MRI arm is small, and the paper says so. Localisation there used gradient-derived pseudo-targets because expert lesion masks were unavailable, and the authors write that prospective validation remains necessary. The abstract names no comparator, so you can't read those numbers against a radiologist.

blocks.headline: Breast MRI segmentation hits 9.7% median volume error but fails to show non-inferiority on treatment-response prediction

lines.text: The second npj Digital Medicine paper matters for what it failed to show. It's an automated segmentation model for breast contrast-enhanced MRI.
Start with what worked.

Across 521 paired internal-test and DUKE cases, median errors were 9.7% for tumour volume, 1.8 millimetres for maximum surface diameter, and 10.2% for enhancement-defined volume. Median Dice was 0.831 internally. In a blinded review by two readers, no major correction was required for 78 of 80 masks.
So the measurement is sound.

The measurement is sound. The prediction is not. In 276 paired response-analysis cases, the area under the curve was 0.732 with automatic geometry against 0.757 with expert geometry, and the paper states that discrimination non-inferiority was not demonstrated. The authors limit their conclusion to radiologist-supervised retrospective research.

blocks.headline: Philippines announces Executive Order 131 creating a National AI Council chaired by the Executive Secretary

lines.text: To policy, and the Philippines. The Manila Times reports that at a press briefing on Saturday, Palace press officer Claire Castro said President Marcos has signed an executive order adopting an artificial intelligence framework, and said that Executive Order 131 places value on AI so that Filipinos may benefit from it.
Who runs it?

Unbox.ph says the order establishes a National AI Council, chaired by Executive Secretary Ralph Recto, with the economy and planning secretary as vice chairperson heading the secretariat, the heads of several other departments and agencies as members, plus a single private-sector representative on a three-year term.

And here's the caveat. The order's text wasn't published on the LawPhil executive-orders index when we checked, so we're reading a palace briefing rather than the document. Neither report gives a signing date, a budget, or a deadline.

blocks.headline: Petition to reinstate Jensen Huang passes 115,000 signatures as two investors ask Nvidia's board to slow its CEO search

lines.text: Compute, and an update on the Nvidia leadership story.

TechCrunch says a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang appears to have attracted more than 115,000 signatures as of Saturday afternoon, and that the petition website lists 5,965 current Nvidia employees, 1,108 former employees and 63,063 shareholders among the signers. Elon Musk is a named supporter.
What about the investors?

CNBC reports that Altimeter's Brad Gerstner posted a letter on X on Friday, co-signed by Atreides' Gavin Baker, urging Nvidia's board to pursue a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.
The two firms disclosed about $2.13 billion of Nvidia stock combined as of June 30th. And neither report explains how the petition verified those employee or shareholder counts.

CNBC also notes a separate letter asking Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify about Megaspeed before the House Intelligence Committee, and that he has agreed to appear before Senate Banking on December 10th.

blocks.headline: FAA administrator says there is "zero evidence of anything AI-related" in the nationwide ground stop, blaming a router after a fibre upgrade

lines.text: An update on Friday's ground stop, and TechCrunch is the one outlet we could open on it.

FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said the agency sees zero evidence of anything nefarious and zero evidence of anything AI-related, and that they have an equipment issue. The ground stop came a day after the FAA announced an AI tool for air traffic controllers, and the controllers' union said it was not consulted in designing it.
So what broke?

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says that during routine maintenance, copper wire at a remote location was upgraded to fibre optic cable by L3Harris, a longtime FAA contractor, and afterwards a router overloaded a critical communication system.

The FAA's acting chief technology officer, Rebecca Guy, said two places were pinging the network at a very high rate — a thousand connections over every four to five seconds. They disabled both. TechCrunch says Cirium counted more than 8,200 flights cancelled on Friday evening, and at least another 3,000 on Saturday.
And no root cause has been published. The denials are statements rather than findings, because the root cause analysis is still running.

blocks.headline: Tesla opens Cybercab pre-orders at $29,990 plus a $299 monthly fee without which the car will not operate

lines.text: Tesla said on Friday evening that select customers can pre-order the Cybercab for personal use. TechCrunch says that on top of the $29,990 price, owners will need to pay $299 per month to operate their vehicle, with delivery estimated for December 2026, and buyers must accept delivery in one of a handful of Texas cities.
And it only drives inside a geofence?

It does. Electrek read the posted autonomy subscription agreement, and the line that matters is this. Your Cybercab will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription. Tesla can change the price with a month's notice, and may expand, reduce, relocate, or otherwise modify the operating area at any time.
What else is in there?

Tesla can remotely access, locate, restrict or control the car, and the agreement says those actions give owners no remedies beyond the terms. It collects autonomy data including cabin camera images, kept 30 days by default. And Elon Musk called the monthly fee too high, saying it should be more like about $115 a month.
Tesla hasn't published that agreement at a stable public address, so those terms come from Electrek's reading of the order page.

blocks.headline: Top scorer in South Korea's tax accountant exam admits using a camera and AI to get answers; police open an investigation

lines.text: And last, South Korea. AFP, carried by The Star, reports that police said on Sunday they had opened an investigation after the top scorer in the national Certified Tax Accountant exam admitted using artificial intelligence to cheat. He scored 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, with a single wrong answer out of 160 questions.
What did he actually do?

In a video on his lawyer's YouTube channel he said he used a miniature camera to photograph the exam questions and sent them to AI, then checked the answers on his smartphone. He said he deeply regretted it, and that he had struggled financially after leaving his job to start a business.
What does the exam body say?

The Human Resources Development Service of Korea says two supervisors were present. It also said on Sunday that an AI inspector caught a test taker wearing smart glasses during a gas engineer certification exam last month. With the Suneung, the national college entrance test, due on November 19th, the presidential office said it is treating the issue seriously.
This is a single source for us — one wire story. And the lawyer said further details won't be disclosed, in case other cheaters copy the method.
That's The AI Edge for today. The full edition is on the site, with a link to every source behind every line, so you can check any of it for yourself.
Our voices are AI-generated. Listen in tomorrow for the next edition.
